abbreviations.expansion: nil per os — nothing by mouth
abbreviations.context: Pre-op and procedure orders. Said as letters: "keep her N-P-O after midnight." From Latin, so don't try to pronounce it as a word.
Tacked onto medication orders: "paracetamol PRN for pain." Spoken either as letters or just said as "as needed."

abbreviations.expansion: bis in die — twice a day
abbreviations.context: Dosing frequency. Often said as letters, "B-I-D," or simply "twice daily." The cousins are QID (four times) and TID (three times).

abbreviations.expansion: ter in die — three times a day
abbreviations.context: Dosing frequency, said as letters. "Start the antibiotic TID." Don't confuse the spoken "T-I-D" with "QID."

abbreviations.expansion: quater in die — four times a day
abbreviations.context: Dosing frequency. Beware the dangerous look-alikes QD (daily) and QOD (every other day), which is why many hospitals now ban them in favor of writing it out.
The urgency flag. Said as a word, "stat": "I need a STAT portable chest film." Reserve it for genuine emergencies or it loses its force.
Route of administration. Said as letters: "switch the antibiotics to P-O once she can eat." Contrasts with IV, IM, SC.
Route — into a vein. Said as letters and used as a noun too: "start an IV," "run it IV." The verb "to cannulate" means placing the IV.
Route — into muscle. "Give the adrenaline I-M." Said as letters; don't confuse with IV when speaking quickly.
Route, said as letters or "sub-Q." Insulin and prophylactic heparin go SC. Also written SQ or subcut.

abbreviations.expansion: ad libitum — as much/often as desired
abbreviations.context: Said as written, "ad lib." Usually about diet or activity: "diet ad lib," "mobilize ad lib." The opposite of a restriction.
Charting shorthand, read aloud as "history." Builds compounds: PMHx (past medical history), FHx (family history), SHx (social history).
Spoken in full as "past medical history" or "past med hist." The patient's prior diagnoses — one of the first things you present.
Said "R-X" or just "treatment." On a chart it heads the drug list; in speech "the Rx" means the plan. The symbol is centuries old.
Read aloud as "diagnosis." Pairs with DDx (the list of possibilities) and Tx (treatment). "What's your working Dx?"
Said "D-D-X" or "the differential." The ranked list of what could be causing the picture: "My DDx is PE, pneumonia, or a flare."
Read aloud as "treatment." "What's the Tx for this?" Sits alongside Dx and Rx in the note shorthand family.
Opens the history: "patient c/o chest pain." Read aloud as "complains of." Neutral charting language, not a comment on the patient.

abbreviations.expansion: status post — in the state following
abbreviations.context: Said "status post." Marks a prior event: "s/p appendectomy" means after an appendix removal. Common in problem lists.
Said "rule out." Names what you're trying to exclude: "admit to r/o MI." A working concern, not a confirmed diagnosis.
Said "workup." The set of tests and steps to investigate a problem: "start the anemia w-u." Also a verb: "work her up for sepsis."

abbreviations.expansion: no acute distress (or no abnormality detected)
abbreviations.context: Two meanings — beware. In US exam notes "NAD" = "no acute distress" (the patient looks comfortable). In UK lab/exam shorthand it can mean "no abnormality detected." Context decides.
Said as letters or "within normal limits." Labels a normal result or finding. The cynical gloss "we never looked" is a warning against overusing it.

abbreviations.expansion: alert and oriented to person, place, and time
abbreviations.context: Said "alert and oriented times three." A quick mental-status snapshot. "Times four" adds awareness of the situation/event.
Said as letters or "review of systems." The head-to-toe symptom checklist taken during history. Distinct from the physical exam.
Said "H-P-I." The narrative of the current problem — the heart of any presentation. "Start your HPI with the one-liner."
Said as a word, "soap note." The standard structure for a progress note. Knowing the four headings keeps your presentations organized.
Said "chief complaint" or "C-C." The patient's main reason for the visit, ideally in their own words: "CC: 'I can't catch my breath.'"
Said "B-P." Spoken as two numbers: 120 over 80, "one-twenty over eighty." "The BP is soft" means it's worryingly low.
Said "H-R" or "heart rate," in beats per minute. "HR's up to 130" flags a tachycardia. Pairs with RR and BP in the vitals string.
Said "R-R." Breaths per minute — the most under-recorded and most useful vital sign. A creeping RR is an early warning of deterioration.
Said "sat" or "O2 sat" or "S-P-O-two." "Sats are 88 on room air" is shorthand everyone understands. "Desatting" means the number is falling.
Said "J-V-P." A bedside read of right-heart filling. "The JVP is up" suggests fluid overload; pairs with JVD (distension).
Said as letters or read out in full. The reassuring lung exam: "chest CTAB." Means no crackles, wheeze, or other added sounds.
Said "R-R-R" or in full. The normal heart exam opener: "heart RRR, no murmurs." Contrasts with "irregularly irregular" for AF.

abbreviations.expansion: pupils equal, round, reactive to light and accommodation
abbreviations.context: Said as a word, "per-la," or spelled out. A compact normal pupil exam. Often trimmed to PERRL when accommodation isn't formally tested.
Said "E-O-M-I." Records normal eye movements: "EOMI, no nystagmus." Part of the cranial-nerve screen.
Said "M-I": "rule out M-I." Subtypes STEMI ("stemmy") and NSTEMI ("non-stemmy") are said as words. One of the most-used abbreviations on any ward.
Said "C-H-F": "known C-H-F, now fluid overloaded." Increasingly just called "heart failure," but the abbreviation is everywhere in older notes.
Said "C-O-P-D." A COPD "exacerbation" is a flare. "He's a retainer" often refers to a COPD patient who holds onto CO2.
Said "C-K-D," usually with a stage: "CKD stage three." Contrast with AKI (the acute, often reversible kind).
Said "A-K-I." The sudden, potentially reversible drop in kidney function. "He's in AKI" triggers a hunt for cause: prerenal, intrinsic, or postrenal.
Said "D-K-A": "she's in D-K-A." A diabetic emergency. The management mantra is fluids, insulin, and potassium watching.
Said "P-E." A clot in the lung. Beware the clash with PE meaning "physical exam" — context disambiguates, but it catches learners out.
Said "D-V-T." A clot in a deep (usually leg) vein, and the upstream source of most PEs. "DVT prophylaxis" is daily ward routine.
Said "C-V-A" or just "stroke." Increasingly replaced by "stroke" in plain communication, but still common in notes and codes.
Said "T-I-A," sometimes "mini-stroke" to patients. Stroke symptoms that fully resolve — a serious warning, not an all-clear.
Said as a word, "gurd." Heartburn's formal name. UK notes write GORD (oesophageal) and say "gord."
Said "U-T-I." Extremely common, especially in older patients where it can present as confusion rather than urinary symptoms.
Said "U-R-I" or "upper respiratory." The common-cold bracket. UK uses URTI. Usually viral and self-limited — a good word to reassure with.
Said "C-B-C." The bread-and-butter blood test (UK: FBC, "full blood count"). "Send a CBC" is reflexive on almost every admission.
Said "B-M-P." Electrolytes plus kidney function and glucose. The broader version is the CMP. "Chem 7" is an older nickname.
Said "C-M-P." The BMP plus liver tests and proteins. "Send a CMP" when you want the wider metabolic picture.
Said "L-F-Ts" ("L-F-tees"). The liver enzyme and bilirubin panel. "Deranged LFTs" is a very common spoken phrase for abnormal results.
Said "A-B-G." The painful-but-vital sample for oxygen, CO2, and pH. "Get a gas" is the standard shorthand. VBG is the gentler venous version.
Said "E-C-G" (UK) or "EKG," "E-K-G" (US, from the German Elektrokardiogramm). "Get a twelve-lead" means a full ECG.
Said "chest X-ray" or "C-X-R." "A portable CXR" is done at the bedside; "PA and lateral" are the standard departmental views.
Said "C-T" or "cat scan." Specify region and contrast: "CT head non-con," "CT-PA" for a pulmonary embolism study.
Said "M-R-I." Higher detail, slower, and contraindicated with certain implants — always screen for metal first.
Said as a word, "echo." Ultrasound of the heart. "TTE" is the standard transthoracic version; "TEE/TOE" is the down-the-throat one.
Said "E-F," a percentage from the echo. "EF of 30" signals a weak pump. The dividing line between preserved and reduced heart failure.
Said "I-N-R." Measures blood thinning on warfarin. "His INR is supratherapeutic" means too thin — bleeding risk.
Said "P-T" and "P-T-T." The two clotting-time tests; PT/INR tracks warfarin, PTT tracks heparin. Order them as "coags."
Said "E-S-R" or "sed rate." A slow, nonspecific inflammation marker. Often paired with CRP: "check an ESR and CRP."
Said "C-R-P." A faster inflammation marker than the ESR. "The CRP is climbing" suggests worsening inflammation or infection.
Said as a word, "bun" (US). A kidney/hydration marker. "The BUN-to-creatinine ratio" helps separate prerenal from intrinsic causes. UK reports urea instead.
Said "G-F-R," usually the estimated version, eGFR. The headline number for kidney function and for dosing drugs safely.
Said "B-N-P." Released by a stretched heart; helps sort cardiac from non-cardiac breathlessness. "A sky-high BNP" points at heart failure.
Usually just said "troponin" or "trop." The marker of heart-muscle damage. "Trend the troponins" means repeat them to watch the curve.
Said "A-one-C" or "hemoglobin A-one-C." A three-month average of blood sugar. "His A1c is nine" signals poor long-term control.
Said "I-C-U." The highest level of ward care. "He needs an ICU bed" is a sentence that changes everyone's pace. UK also says ITU.
Said "E-D" (US) or "A and E" (UK, accident and emergency). "Came in through the ED" is the standard phrasing for an emergency presentation.
Said "O-R" (US) or "theatre" (UK). "Take her to the OR" means surgery now. "Book the OR" schedules it.
Said as a word, "pack-you," or "recovery." Where patients wake up after surgery before going back to the ward.
Said "L and D." The obstetric unit where deliveries happen. UK equivalent is "the labour ward" or "delivery suite."
Said as a word, "nick-you." Intensive care for newborns. Distinct from PICU ("pick-you"), the pediatric unit for older children.
Said "D-N-R." An order against CPR if the heart stops. Increasingly written DNACPR. A sensitive conversation, not just a checkbox.
Said "D-N-I." An order against placing a breathing tube. Often paired with DNR but distinct — a patient can be DNI without being DNR.
Said "A-M-A": "he left AMA." When a patient discharges themselves despite advice. Distinct from the UK's similar "LAMA" (left against medical advice).
Said "follow-up." The plan to review the patient later: "f/u in clinic in two weeks." Both a noun and a verb in ward speech.
Dangerously ambiguous — said "discharge" or "D-C." "D/C the patient" means send home; "d/c the heparin" means stop the drug. Many hospitals now ban it for exactly this reason; write the word out.
Read aloud as "symptoms." Part of the x-shorthand family with Hx, Dx, Tx. Occasionally means surgery — context tells you which.
Read aloud as "biopsy." "Send it for Bx" means take a tissue sample. Fits the same shorthand pattern as Dx and Tx.
Read aloud as "fracture." "Hip Fx" on the board means a broken hip. Common in orthopedics and emergency notes.
Said "a-b-x" or just "antibiotics." "Start broad-spectrum abx" is daily ward language. "De-escalate the abx" once cultures return.
Said "N-K-D-A" or in full. A safety check recorded on every drug chart. "NKDA" lets you prescribe with one less worry.
Said "packed cells" or "P-R-B-Cs." The blood product given to raise hemoglobin. "Transfuse two units of packed cells."
Said "ins and outs" or "I and O." Tracking fluid in versus urine out — crucial in heart and kidney patients. "Strict I&O" means measure everything.
Said "N-G": "drop an N-G tube." Goes through the nose to the stomach for feeding or drainage. "NG to suction" decompresses a blocked gut.
Said as a name, "Foley." The balloon-tipped bladder catheter. "Place a Foley" to monitor urine output hourly; remove it early to avoid infection.
Said "L-P" or "spinal tap." Sampling spinal fluid, classically to investigate meningitis. "Do an LP" usually follows the question of infection or bleeding.
Said as a word, "rosk." The moment a pulse comes back during a resuscitation: "we got ROSC after two cycles." The goal of every code.
Said "B-I-B-A" (UK). Opens many emergency notes: "BIBA following a collapse." Tells you how the patient arrived.

abbreviations.expansion: per vaginam — via the vaginal route
abbreviations.context: Said "P-V." Used for exams, bleeding, or medication routes in obstetrics and gynecology: "PV bleeding," "give it PV." From Latin, like PO and PR.

abbreviations.expansion: per rectum — via the rectal route
abbreviations.context: Said "P-R." A route and an exam: "PR bleeding," "do a PR exam." Watch for the unrelated PR meaning on an ECG (the PR interval).
